{
  "essay": "It is often argued that governments should allocate more funding to public transport instead of constructing new roads. While I partly agree that public transport deserves greater investment, I believe that new roads remain necessary in some circumstances.\n\nThere are strong reasons why public transport should receive more funding. Many people, particularly students and low-income residents, do not own a car and rely on buses and trains to travel to work or school. If services were more frequent, affordable and comfortable, more commuters would choose them, which would reduce traffic congestion. In my city, for example, buses are often late and overcrowded, and train fares are too high for students, so few people are willing to use them. Governments should therefore make public transport cheaper, more reliable and faster.\n\nHowever, building new roads is also important. As cities expand and car ownership rises, the existing road network cannot cope with the growing volume of traffic. Without new roads, congestion would become severe and commuters would waste hours in traffic jams. For instance, my father drives to work every day and spends two hours on the road, which harms both his well-being and the local economy.\n\nNevertheless, I believe public transport is the higher priority. Building more roads tends to encourage greater car use and thus more pollution, whereas public transport can carry large numbers of passengers at once and is therefore better for the environment. Moreover, if more people took buses and trains, cities would be quieter and the air cleaner, which would benefit everyone's health.\n\nIn conclusion, although I agree that governments should invest more in public transport, new roads should still be built where they are genuinely necessary, since both are important for citizens and for national development.",
  "key_changes": [
    "将开头段改写为清晰的立场表达：部分同意公共交通优先，但认为新道路在必要时仍不可少，回应了题目中“to what extent”的要求。",
    "把原文零散的观点按“支持公共交通—道路的必要性—为何公共交通优先—结论”重组为四个主体段落，每段一个中心论点，逻辑更连贯。",
    "修正全部语法错误（如 I am agree、more better、the city is grow、Both is important 等），并替换口语化表达（如 very important problem、go work）为学术书面语。",
    "保留学生原有例子（家乡公交晚点拥挤、学生票价高、父亲通勤两小时），但补充解释其与论点的关系，使论证更充分。",
    "结尾段明确综合双方观点，给出有条件的结论，避免原文结论含糊的问题。"
  ],
  "band_rationale": "该版本达到 Band 7：任务回应上明确表达部分同意的立场，每个主体段都有清晰的中心句和展开论证，例子与论点衔接紧密；连贯与衔接上分段合理，使用 While、However、Nevertheless、Moreover 等衔接手段，逻辑推进自然；词汇资源上使用了 allocate funding、commuters、congestion、car ownership、higher priority 等较多样且准确的表达，偶有搭配仍属常见但无误；语法上句式有变化（条件句、定语从句、比较结构），错误基本消除，符合 Band 7 对“频繁无错句”的要求。"
}

{
  "essay": "In many cities, traffic congestion has become a serious problem, and governments must decide how to allocate limited budgets. Some people argue that money should be spent on public transport rather than on building new roads. I largely agree with this view, although I believe that some road construction remains necessary.\n\nThe main reason to invest in public transport is that it can move large numbers of people efficiently. A single train can carry hundreds of passengers, whereas the same number of people would require hundreds of cars. If buses and trains are frequent, affordable and reliable, many drivers will choose them, which will reduce traffic jams. For example, after my city opened a new metro line, the main road to the city centre became much less congested during rush hour.\n\nAnother advantage is environmental. Cars produce significant air pollution and carbon emissions, which harm people's health and contribute to climate change. Public transport generates less pollution per passenger, making it a more sustainable option in the long term.\n\nOn the other hand, new roads are sometimes needed. In rural areas, there are not enough passengers to make train lines profitable, so people depend on cars. Moreover, goods are mostly transported by trucks, and poor roads can slow down the economy.\n\nIn conclusion, I agree that governments should give priority to public transport because it is more efficient and better for the environment. However, they should still build roads in places where public transport is not practical.",
  "key_changes": [
    "将原文中零散的逻辑连接词（如“On the other hand”）保留并优化，使段落间过渡更自然，例如在第二段开头明确“The main reason”以突出论点。",
    "修正了部分表达不够学术的问题，如将“money should go to”改为“money should be spent on”，将“less crowded”改为“less congested”，提升词汇的正式度。",
    "调整了句子结构，使长句更流畅，例如将“If buses and trains are frequent, cheap and reliable, many drivers will choose them, which will reduce traffic jams”改为更紧凑的表述，并保留例子。",
    "将“Another advantage is the environment”改为“Another advantage is environmental”，使语法更准确。",
    "在结论段强化了立场的一致性，明确“give priority to public transport”并补充“where public transport is not practical”，使论证更完整。"
  ],
  "band_rationale": "该版本达到Band 7，因为：1）任务回应：明确表达立场（largely agree），并充分讨论双方观点，给出例子和让步，符合7分要求；2）连贯与衔接：段落清晰，逻辑连接词使用恰当，信息组织合理；3）词汇资源：使用了一些不太常见的词汇（如congested, allocate, sustainable），且搭配基本准确；4）语法多样性与准确性：使用了复杂句式（如条件句、定语从句），语法错误极少。整体语言自然，符合学术写作规范。"

{
  "essay": "As urban populations grow, governments face a difficult choice about where to direct transport spending. While some advocate building more roads to ease congestion, I largely agree that public transport deserves the greater share of investment, because it addresses the causes of traffic problems rather than merely their symptoms.\n\nThe strongest argument for prioritising public transport is efficiency. Roads are an inherently limited resource: a lane of motorway can carry only a fixed number of private vehicles per hour, whereas a well-run rail or bus rapid transit line can move many times that number of people in the same space. Moreover, there is considerable evidence that new roads tend to fill up quickly, as cheaper and faster journeys encourage more people to drive. Expanding road networks may therefore offer only temporary relief before congestion returns.\n\nPublic transport also brings wider social and environmental benefits. It gives affordable mobility to those who cannot drive, such as students, the elderly and lower-income workers, thereby widening their access to jobs and services. At the same time, shifting journeys from cars to trains and buses reduces both air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions, which is increasingly important as cities attempt to meet climate targets.\n\nNevertheless, it would be unrealistic to stop road building altogether. In sparsely populated regions, buses and trains are rarely viable, and freight still relies heavily on trucks. Targeted road improvements, such as bypasses around congested towns, can therefore remain a sensible use of funds.\n\nIn conclusion, although some road investment is still justified, governments should concentrate their spending on public transport, since it offers a more lasting solution to congestion while also delivering social and environmental gains.",

{
  "essay": "How a government allocates its transport budget shapes not only how quickly people travel, but also the kind of cities they live in. Although building new roads has an intuitive appeal whenever traffic worsens, I am convinced that investment should be weighted decisively towards public transport, with road construction reserved for cases where no realistic alternative exists.\n\nThe case for new roads rests largely on the assumption that congestion is simply a shortage of capacity. Yet experience from many large cities suggests otherwise: widening a motorway lowers the cost of driving, which in turn draws additional traffic until the new lanes are as clogged as the old ones. This phenomenon, often described as induced demand, means that road building can become an expensive treadmill. Public transport, by contrast, increases the number of people a corridor can carry without a proportional increase in the space consumed, and a single metro line can relieve pressure on an entire network of streets.\n\nEqually important are the distributional consequences. Road spending disproportionately benefits those who own cars, whereas frequent and affordable buses and trains extend opportunity to people who cannot or prefer not to drive. Well-designed transit also allows denser, more walkable neighbourhoods to develop around stations, reducing the distances people need to travel in the first place, and it cuts emissions at a time when the transport sector remains one of the most stubborn sources of carbon.\n\nThat said, a blanket refusal to build roads would be misguided. Rural communities and freight logistics depend on reliable highways, and in such contexts targeted upgrades may represent genuine value for money.\n\nOn balance, therefore, public transport should receive the lion's share of funding, because it tackles congestion at its root and produces broader social and environmental returns that new roads rarely match.",

{
  "essay": "Online learning has expanded rapidly over the past decade, and some people now argue that it will eventually replace traditional classrooms. In my view, although online courses offer clear advantages, face-to-face education will remain essential.\n\nThe most obvious benefit of online learning is flexibility. Students can watch lectures at any time and study at their own pace, which is particularly useful for adults who work full-time or have family responsibilities. Online courses can also reach learners in remote areas who would otherwise have no access to qualified teachers. In addition, digital materials can be updated quickly, and learners can replay difficult explanations as many times as they need, which is impossible in a traditional lecture. For many people, these features make online study cheaper and more convenient than attending a college in person.\n\nHowever, classroom learning provides benefits that are difficult to replicate on a screen. Teachers can immediately notice when a student is confused and adjust their explanations accordingly. Students also develop social skills by working together, discussing ideas and building friendships, which are an important part of education, particularly for children.\n\nFurthermore, many learners find it hard to stay motivated without the structure of a timetable and the presence of classmates. While I largely agree that investment in buses and trains should take precedence, I believe that some road building remains necessary in certain areas.\n\nThe main argument for spending on public transport is its efficiency. A single bus or train can carry dozens or even hundreds of passengers at once, whereas private cars usually transport only one or two people. As a result, expanding bus and rail networks can significantly reduce congestion in large cities, where traffic jams waste both time and fuel. Public transport is also more affordable for students and elderly people who do not own a car, giving them access to jobs, education and healthcare.
